bib.title: Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less. Silei Xu, Wenhao Xie, Lingxiao Zhao, Pengcheng He (Zoom Communications). arXiv:2502.18600v2, 3 Mar 2025 (arXiv preprint, cs.CL; no venue printed).

COVERAGE: 27,433 of 27,433 chars read, all 7 pages. No gaps. There are no appendices. The text contains no embedded instructions. I did not run the figures script. Figure 1 is a chart whose data is not in the extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. CoD (Chain of Draft) matches or beats CoT in accuracy on some tasks while using far fewer tokens.
 - number: as little as 7.6% of the tokens
 - setup: few-shot, GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620). Tasks are GSM8k, BIG-bench date and sports understanding, and coin flip. The 7.6% figure is not tied to a specific table. It is consistent with Claude on sports, where CoD uses 14.3 tokens against 189.4 for CoT (14.3/189.4 = 7.55%, my arithmetic).
 - quote: "CoD matches or surpasses CoT in accuracy while using as little as only 7.6% of the tokens, significantly reducing cost and latency across various reasoning tasks."
 - where: abstract, p.1

2. On GSM8K, CoD gives up about 4 points of accuracy against CoT. It cuts output tokens by about 80% and latency by 76.2% (GPT-4o) and 48.4% (Claude).
 - number: GPT-4o 95.4% / 205.1 tokens / 4.2 s (CoT) against 91.1% / 43.9 / 1.0 s (CoD). Claude 3.5 Sonnet 95.8% / 190.0 / 3.1 s (CoT) against 91.4% / 39.8 / 1.6 s (CoD). Standard prompting gets 53.3% (GPT-4o) and 64.6% (Claude) at 1.1 tokens.
 - setup: few-shot, Table 1. Latency is in seconds, with no hardware or API conditions stated.
 - quote: "CoD achieves an accuracy of 91% for both models while requiring only about 40 tokens per response, thereby reducing the average output token count by 80% and cutting the average latency by 76.2% and 48.4%, respectively."
 - where: Sec 4.2, Table 1, p.4

3. On date understanding, CoD is close to CoT for GPT-4o and better for Claude. Token savings are 60% (GPT-4o) and 82% (Claude), my arithmetic from the table.
 - number: GPT-4o CoT 90.2% / 75.7 tokens / 1.7 s, CoD 88.1% / 30.2 / 1.3 s. Claude CoT 87.0% / 172.5 / 3.2 s, CoD 89.7% / 31.3 / 1.4 s. Standard gets 72.6% (GPT-4o) and 84.3% (Claude).
 - setup: BIG-bench date understanding, few-shot, Table 2.
 - quote: "CoD outperforms CoT in accuracy in various cases."
 - where: Sec 4.3, Table 2

4. On sports understanding, CoD beats CoT in accuracy and uses far fewer tokens.
 - number: GPT-4o CoT 95.9% / 28.7 tokens / 0.9 s, CoD 98.3% / 15.0 / 0.7 s. Claude CoT 93.2% / 189.4 / 3.6 s, CoD 97.3% / 14.3 / 1.0 s. Standard gets 90.0% (GPT-4o) and 90.6% (Claude). The text states a 92.4% token reduction for Claude.
 - setup: BIG-bench sports understanding, few-shot, Table 3.
 - quote: "CoD reduces the average output tokens from 189.4 to 14.3 — a 92.4% reduction."
 - where: Sec 4.3, Table 3 (Table 3 is on p.4 and p.5 in the extraction)

5. On coin flip, CoT and CoD both reach 100%, and CoD uses fewer tokens.
 - number: GPT-4o CoT 52.4 tokens / 1.4 s, CoD 16.8 / 0.8 s. Claude CoT 135.3 / 3.1 s, CoD 18.9 / 1.6 s. Standard gets 73.2% (GPT-4o) and 85.2% (Claude).
 - setup: 250 synthetic examples, because "the exact dataset is not published". Each uses 4 names from the top 1000 US first names (NameDataset), each randomly flipping or not. Table 4.
 - quote: "both models reach a perfect 100% accuracy with CoT and CoD. Again, CoD demonstrates significant reduction of tokens compared to CoT, from 68% for GPT-4o to 86% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet."
 - where: Sec 4.4, Table 4

6. Zero-shot, CoD degrades sharply. The few-shot CoD examples are necessary.
 - number: GSM8K zero-shot. GPT-4o Standard 56.9%, CoT 94.8% / 278.4 tokens / 8.1 s, CoD 84.4% / 76.4 / 2.6 s. Claude Standard 61.9%, CoT 90.4% / 248.8 / 3.5 s, CoD 65.5% / 73.7 / 1.6 s.
 - setup: GSM8K with no few-shot examples, Table 5. The authors "hypothesize" the cause is that CoD-style patterns are scarce in training data. This is not tested.
 - quote: "for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, CoD improved performance over direct answering by only 3.6%. Additionally, the token savings achieved by CoD are less significant compared to few-shot setting."
 - where: Sec 4.5, Table 5, p.5

7. Small models (under 3B parameters) show a larger gap between CoD and CoT.
 - number (GSM8K accuracy / tokens):

| Model | Standard | CoT | CoD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-1.5B | 5.7% | 32.5% / 141.4 | 24.2% / 75.1 |
| Qwen2.5-3B | 7.2% | 59.1% / 236.4 | 43.1% / 41.2 |
| Llama3.2-3B | 3.9% | 70.7% / 195.3 | 52.5% / 98.1 |
| Zoom-SLM-2.3B | 5.9% | 77.7% / 129.0 | 50.9% / 55.6 |

 - setup: Table 6. No latency column. The authors suspect missing CoD-style training data and anticipate that fine-tuning on CoD data would help. They did not test this.
 - quote: "While CoD effectively reduces the number of tokens required per response and improves accuracy over direct answer, its performance gap compared to CoT is more pronounced in these models."
 - where: Sec 4.5, Table 6

8. CoD sets a per-step word limit (5 words), unlike a global budget. This allows unlimited steps. It also shortens the few-shot prompt, which lowers input cost.
 - number: 5 words per step. The limit is a guideline and is not enforced.
 - quote: "Note that we do not enforce such limitation in any way, it is just a general guideline to promte short reasoning steps."
 - where: Sec 4.1 (prompt) and Sec 2 (per-step vs global budget) and Sec 5 (input cost)
 - Related quote on input cost: "it reduces the number of input tokens required for few-shot prompting and shortens the output token length".

9. Prompts used. The CoD system prompt is "Think step by step, but only keep a minimum draft for each thinking step, with 5 words at most. Return the answer at the end of the response after a separator ####." The CoT prompt is "Think step by step to answer the following question. Return the answer at the end of the response after a separator ####." The Standard prompt is "Answer the question directly. Do not return any preamble, explanation, or reasoning." The CoT few-shot examples are the exact ones from Wei et al. 2022, with the answer after "####". The CoD few-shot examples were written manually by the authors.
 - where: Sec 4.1

LIMITS
- Only two proprietary models are used: GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
- Only four tasks are used, all older and relatively easy. There is no code, no hard math (MATH, AIME), and no reasoning models.
- No variance, seeds or confidence intervals are reported. The coin flip set is synthetic with n=250. Test-set sizes for the other tasks are not stated.
- Latency is a single average with no hardware or API detail. Latency gains are smaller than token gains for Claude, for example 3.1 s to 1.6 s on GSM8K.
- The authors concede CoD is inconsistent without few-shot examples and weaker on models under 3B. Their explanations are hypotheses only.
- No comparison with CCoT or TALE is run, despite them being named as the closest work.
- The draft word limit is not enforced. The paper does not measure how often models comply.
- The paper does not say whether the CoD examples' hand-written quality affects results. There is no ablation of the 5-word limit.
- Dated: the models are mid-2024 versions. Reasoning models (o1, R1) are mentioned but not evaluated.

BUILDS ON
- Wei et al., 2022 (CoT, few-shot examples reused)
- Kojima et al., 2022
- Cobbe et al., 2021 (GSM8k)
- BIG-bench authors, 2023
- Brown et al., 2020 (few-shot)
- Closest work: Nayab et al., 2024 (Concise Thoughts, CCoT) and Han et al., 2024 (TALE, token-budget-aware reasoning)
- Other related work: Wang et al., 2022 (self-consistency); Yao et al., 2022 (ReAct); Yao et al., 2024 (Tree of Thoughts); Besta et al., 2024 (Graph of Thoughts); Ning et al., 2023 (Skeleton-of-Thought); Zhang et al., 2023 (Draft & Verify); Hao et al., 2024 (Coconut); Wang et al., 2024 (budget-aware evaluation); Chen et al., 2024b and Chiang and Lee, 2024 (overthinking)

CODE: none beyond the prompts above. A code repository is cited: https://github.com/sileix/chain-of-draft

Worked example (Sec 3, p.3):
- Chain of Draft answer: "A: 20 - x = 12; x = 20 - 12 = 8. #### 8"
- The CoT answer for the same problem runs six numbered steps.

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.1): Claude 3.5 Sonnet accuracy and token usage for Standard, CoT and CoD across tasks. It gives a quick visual of "similar accuracy, far fewer tokens". Its data points are not in the extracted text, so cite the tables instead.

PROBLEMS: None significant. The extraction is clean text. Table 3 (sports) is split across a page break, so its header row appears after the coin-flip text begins. The paper has typos ("Limitaitons", "promte"). Table 2 is the date table, so the paper's table numbering is not by task order.
